Paul Ehrlich. The German physician and biochemist who pioneered chemotherapy, the use of synthetic chemicals to treat disease. He synthesized over 600 compounds before discovering arsphenamine, also known as Salvarsan, which became the first effective treatment for syphilis and marked a paradigm shift in medicine.

Ehrlich developed arsphenamine in 1909, making it the first truly effective synthetic antimicrobial drug. He articulated the concept of the magic bullet, from the German Zauberkugel, which expressed the ideal of a drug molecule that destroys disease agents with minimal harm to the patient. This vision would guide medicine for generations to come.

His early work pioneered staining techniques for bacteria and cells. These techniques were revolutionary for their time, helping bacteriology move from simple observation to a system of classification. Ehrlich also postulated the existence of receptors on cell surfaces. While these were not directly observable in his era, he theorized them as the mediators of drug action and natural immunity, an insight that proved prophetic.

Beyond his chemical work, Ehrlich made contributions to serology and immunity, particularly in studying complement, the proteins in blood that enhance immune response. He founded the science of chemotherapy itself, establishing the principle that disease treatment should depend on systematic chemical synthesis, testing, and refinement rather than relying on serendipitous discovery alone. In 1905, Ehrlich shared the Nobel Prize with Robert Koch, who had identified the pathogens; together they showed that medicine now had the tools to chemically attack them.
